momentum_panic_state.note: Daniel & Moskowitz (2016): after a 24-month market decline with high 126-day variance, momentum is prone to crash — on sharp REBOUNDS, when past losers rally hardest. Not an index direction call.

rows.label: High-yield spread (OAS)
rows.note: ICE BofA US High Yield OAS via FRED — published with a one-day lag.

rows.label: VIX curve (VIX ÷ VIX3M)
rows.note: Level, not change: below 0.90 = calm contango; 1.00 or above = inverted (near-term fear priced above 3-month).

diagnosis.label: No significant equity stress
diagnosis.summary: The index move is within about 1σ of its recent volatility.

points.value: HY spread +6 bp vs +4 bp implied by the equity move (excess +2 bp, +0.3σ); FRED through 2026-10-16
Treasuries +1.20% while stocks fell — bonds hedging, but no extreme flight-to-safety day
1-year stock–bond correlation +0.27: bonds have not been hedging stocks (inflation / real-rate regime)
Equal-weight +0.95 pts vs S&P — selling concentrated in mega-caps

diagnosis.rules: Broad risk-off = S&P ≤ −1σ AND credit confirming (HY spread widening ≥1.5σ beyond what the equity move implies — equities lead credit) AND VIX ≥ VIX3M. Stress building = S&P ≤ −1σ and credit or the VIX curve partly confirming. Equity-only = S&P ≤ −1σ with calm credit and VIX contango. Flight to safety = Baele et al. (2020) joint-tail test. Carry unwind = yen ≤ −1.5% AND VIX ≥ +1σ.

calibration.method: Replayed from 2000 with no look-ahead (expanding feature scaling, only analogs whose outcome was known, as-of base rate). Shrinkage tuned on 2000–2012; skill measured on 2013 onward. Brier skill vs the base rate with a moving-block bootstrap 95% CI.

path.baseline_note: Baselines: every 3rd day since 1990 (new low, worst close, first passage); every 3rd day that was itself down over 3 sessions (reclaim).

analogs.method: k-nearest historical days (S&P 500 since 1990) on: 3-session move in σ, last-session move in σ, drawdown from 52-week high, distance to 200-day, log VIX. Forward windows of the kept matches never overlap, so n counts independent episodes.

options_cone.method: SPY at-the-money straddle per expiry → implied 1σ = straddle·√(π/2)/spot; total variance interpolated linearly in calendar days; lognormal percentiles. Risk-neutral: implied vol usually runs above realized, and skew is ignored.

tells.label: Breaks the last session's low
tells.detail: A lower low after a lower close means the selloff is still finding sellers.

evidence.note: A price level, not a forecast: it tells you whether the selloff is still finding sellers.

tells.label: VIX curve inverts (VIX ≥ VIX3M)
tells.detail: Near-term fear priced above 3-month fear is the classic panic signature.

evidence.note: A stress gauge: inversion marks higher realized volatility, but mainly predicts VIX products, not the index. 'Backwardation marks the bottom' is folklore — above 1.10 the outcomes were two-sided.

tells.label: Credit widens beyond what the equity move implies
tells.detail: HY spread +6 bp vs +4 bp expected from the S&P (+0.3σ). Spreads that widen MORE than stocks imply turn a pullback into a funding problem.

evidence.note: Equities lead credit by a day or more (strong evidence), so spreads confirm rather than predict. 'Credit not confirming means all clear' is contradicted. The page's excess-widening rule is moderate.

tells.label: Closes below the 50-day average
tells.detail: Losing the trend average shifts the regime from pullback to correction.

evidence.note: Moving-average signals forecast monthly returns out of sample, mostly in recessions; bull/correction/bear/rebound states carry information. The best rules were insignificant out of sample in 1987–96.

tells.label: Yen surges with a VIX jump (carry unwind)
tells.detail: USD/JPY −1.5% or more in 3 sessions AND VIX up ≥1σ. A yen rally alone is a safe-haven flow; together with a vol spike it forces carry-trade unwinds that spill into equities.

evidence.note: Unwinds cluster with a rising VIX, but there is roughly one recent episode and no study of forward returns; a yen rally on its own is an ordinary safe-haven flow.

tells.label: Takes back the last session's high
tells.detail: Reversing the whole last selloff day shows buyers absorbed the supply.

evidence.note: A price level, not a forecast: it tells you whether the selloff is still finding sellers.

tells.label: Reclaims the pre-selloff close
tells.detail: Erases the 3-session move — a full V-recovery.

evidence.note: A price level, not a forecast: it tells you whether the selloff is still finding sellers.

tells.label: VIX curve back in contango (< 0.90)
tells.detail: Near-term vol priced well below 3-month vol means the market isn't paying up for protection.

evidence.note: A stress gauge: inversion marks higher realized volatility, but mainly predicts VIX products, not the index. 'Backwardation marks the bottom' is folklore — above 1.10 the outcomes were two-sided.

tells.label: Credit no worse than the equity move implies
tells.detail: Equity selloffs that credit doesn't amplify have tended to stay equity-only.

evidence.note: Equities lead credit by a day or more (strong evidence), so spreads confirm rather than predict. 'Credit not confirming means all clear' is contradicted. The page's excess-widening rule is moderate.

tells.label: Equal-weight beats cap-weight on the bounce
tells.detail: A bounce led by the average stock (RSP > SPY) is broader and more durable than a mega-cap squeeze. Value shown = last session's RSP − SPY.

evidence.note: Broad participation predicts continuation at MONTHLY horizons across 64 markets, with little short-term power. 'Narrow breadth means a drawdown is coming' rests on industry research only.

context_notes.label: Estimated dealer gamma: short (convention-based, SPY)
context_notes.detail: When dealers are short gamma, intraday moves have tended to extend into the close, and that extension has reverted over the following days (Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens 2021). A volatility read, not a direction call. Caveat: the public-data sign rule (dealers long calls, short puts) overstates 'short gamma' — signed S&P option data show dealers net long gamma most of the time — so treat the sign as uncertain; gamma walls and the flip level have no peer-reviewed support as price targets.

evidence.note: Volatility only; sign uncertain. Baltussen et al. 2021 (JFE); Amaya et al. 2025; Adams et al. (draft).

evidence.bottom_line: After a sharp selloff, research reliably predicts that volatility stays high and the range of outcomes widens. The direction of the next move is only weakly and conditionally predictable.

grades.strong: Peer-reviewed, long samples, replicated or validated out of sample.
grades.moderate: Peer-reviewed but a single study, no clean out-of-sample test, or a horizon that doesn't match 1–20 sessions.
grades.weak: Practitioner backtests, small or in-sample evidence, or construction practice with no predictive validation.
grades.folklore: No independent test was found — or the evidence contradicts the claim.

items.finding: Declines raise future volatility more than equal rallies, and that forecast holds out of sample from 1 day to 3 months. Expected returns do not rise in step, and turning it into a timing rule failed out of sample across 103 strategies.
items.on_page: The fan's width and both tails are the most reliable output on this page.

items.finding: The S&P 500's 5-day autocorrelation measure flipped from +0.050 to −0.141 after 1999, so partial bounces over 1–5 sessions became modestly more likely — strongest when volatility and volume are high.
items.on_page: Analogs are split before / since 2000 in 'What happened after similar setups'.

items.signal: Most return predictors fail out of sample
items.finding: Predictors usually fail to beat the historical average out of sample; shrinkage recovers a little. Overlapping windows overstate significance, and with 40 analogs a 10-point edge is detected only 28% of the time.
items.on_page: Walk-forward track record, episode-robust ranges, Holm-adjusted badges and a best estimate shrunk to the base rate.

items.signal: Momentum crashes (the factor, not the index)
items.finding: Crashes of past winners are forecastable from a bear-market, high-variance state — and they happen on index REBOUNDS, when past losers rally hardest. There is no evidence on what the index does after crowded-long selling days.
items.on_page: Momentum panic-state line; 'Crowded-long selling' vs 'Short squeeze / junk rally' labels.

items.finding: Equities lead credit by a day or more (strong evidence), so spreads confirm rather than predict. 'Credit not confirming means all clear' is contradicted. The page's excess-widening rule is moderate.
items.on_page: Credit counts only when it widens beyond what the equity move implies; FRED's one-day lag is flagged.

items.finding: Moving-average signals forecast monthly returns out of sample, mostly in recessions; bull/correction/bear/rebound states carry information. The best rules were insignificant out of sample in 1987–96.
items.on_page: The 200-day / 50-day tell and the trend chip.

items.finding: It is a risk-neutral price of insurance: too wide in calm markets and too narrow at 1 day after crashes. Risk-adjusted option densities pass calibration tests; raw ones don't.
items.on_page: The amber lines on the fan; coverage of a VIX-implied cone is shown from this page's own replay.

items.finding: The public sign rule is validated only for end-of-day continuation that reverts over the next days; signed S&P data show dealers net long gamma 88% of the time, so the sign is uncertain.
items.on_page: A volatility-regime note — not a tell, not a direction call. Dealer levels are off by default.

items.finding: Flights to safety occur on under 2% of days; 62% last one day and none more than 10. Positive stock–bond correlation goes with inflation regimes, when bonds stop hedging.
items.on_page: The joint-tail flight-to-safety test and the stock–bond correlation line in the stress diagnosis.

items.finding: High-volume declines are more likely to be followed by higher expected returns; no effect size exists for 1–20-day S&P analogs.
items.on_page: Not used yet — a candidate feature that must pass the walk-forward test first.

items.finding: A stress gauge: inversion marks higher realized volatility, but mainly predicts VIX products, not the index. 'Backwardation marks the bottom' is folklore — above 1.10 the outcomes were two-sided.
items.on_page: The VIX-curve tells and stress-grid row, graded as a regime gauge.

items.finding: Broad participation predicts continuation at MONTHLY horizons across 64 markets, with little short-term power. 'Narrow breadth means a drawdown is coming' rests on industry research only.
items.on_page: 'Who is participating' panel, new-highs/new-lows and equal-weight tells — descriptive context.

items.finding: Unwinds cluster with a rising VIX, but there is roughly one recent episode and no study of forward returns; a yen rally on its own is an ordinary safe-haven flow.
items.on_page: The carry-unwind tell needs a yen surge AND a VIX jump.

items.finding: The grid's cut-offs are conventions; composite stress indices are well built but have no peer-reviewed 1–20-day S&P forecasting record.
items.on_page: The stress grid and diagnosis describe how broad the stress is — not what comes next.

items.finding: In-sample and descriptive (13 independent episodes at VIX ≥ 40), with the spread widening too; rigorous tests find no 1–3-month power for the VIX level.

items.signal: Gamma flip / walls as support; post-opex 'unclench'
items.finding: Vendor claims only; the S&P index basket shows no pinning from SPX expirations.
items.on_page: Dealer levels are labelled estimates and hidden by default; expiry notes are neutral.

items.finding: No peer-reviewed out-of-sample test; calibrated on NYSE data, not S&P 500 members (about 20 Zweig signals since 1945).
items.on_page: Shown as practitioner tells with this grade.

events.note: VIX futures/options settle. 'Vanna/charm' flow stories around it are practitioner lore without peer-reviewed support.

read: The S&P 500 fell 0.11% over the last 3 sessions (-0.1σ vs. its prior 60-session volatility); it is 1.4% below its 52-week high and 6.0% above its 200-day average.

In the 40 closest historical setups since 1990 (from 28 distinct episodes), the index was higher 5 sessions later 60% of the time (episode-robust 95% range 41–78%) vs. 58% for any day — no edge vs. any day. The 10th-percentile 5-session outcome was -3.3% (any day: -2.5%). Over 20 sessions: 58% higher vs. 64% for any day — leans toward further losses, but not distinguishable from chance at this sample size.

After those setups the index traded below the last session's low within 5 sessions 60% of the time (any day: 68%) and fully recovered the 3-session move within 20 sessions 85% of the time (any down-3-session day: 78%).

Track record: replayed since 2000 with no hindsight, this analog engine's 5-session odds after selloffs have not beaten the plain base rate (Brier skill -0.5%, 95% CI -8.0% to +5.3%, 240 test origins). Read the history numbers as what happened, not a forecast; the calibrated best estimate of P(up) is 58%.
The raw history fan held only 64% of 5-session outcomes after selloffs (target 80%), so it is drawn widened ×1.23; a VIX-implied cone held 90% — options ranges usually run wide.
Options price a ±0.9% 1σ move for the next session and ±1.7% over 5 sessions.
No significant equity stress: The index move is within about 1σ of its recent volatility.
